title: Diffraction-quality crystals of arbitrary macromolecules on demand

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a transferable nucleant, surface, or crystallization protocol that predictably produces crystals suitable for structural diffraction experiments from diverse purified macromolecules, including targets that have resisted ordinary screening. A nucleant provides a place where crystal formation can begin; the intended advance must also produce sufficiently ordered crystals for useful measurements. Merely inducing precipitation or the first signs of crystallization would not fulfill the concept.

Proposed scope: the method would work across previously refractory soluble proteins, macromolecular complexes, and a defined class of membrane proteins without requiring a newly engineered construct for every target. Membrane proteins would need explicitly specified compatible environments, potentially including bilayer-like preparations. The supplied evidence does not establish this membrane coverage. The title expresses the ultimate ambition; reproducible success across a broad, defined panel would be a substantial advance even if literal applicability to arbitrary macromolecules remained unproven.

significance.text: Suitable crystals remain a major sample-preparation bottleneck for macromolecular diffraction. The 2025 review describes crystallography's continuing value for high-resolution protein and protein–ligand structures alongside cryo-electron microscopy. A predictable way to obtain usable crystals from previously inaccessible targets would remove this particular barrier and expand the set of biological systems available for crystallographic investigation. The revolutionary consequence would be transferability: difficult targets could enter experiments through a repeatable preparation method instead of requiring a separate crystallization discovery effort for each one.

Conditional downstream possibilities include broader ligand-complex studies, fragment screening, protonation measurements, and time-resolved experiments. These are potential applications identified in the research, rather than capabilities demonstrated by the supplied evidence. Crystallization alone would not guarantee them: crystals must also provide adequate resolution, permit the relevant ligand access or reaction, and suit the required measurement methods. Removing the crystallization barrier would enable attempts at these experiments, while leaving their other scientific and instrumental requirements intact.

Impact limits: this innovation would complement methods that obtain structural information without crystals, rather than establish that crystallography should replace them. It would not, by itself, recover a unique native fold for an intrinsically disordered protein with no stable domain; such proteins are excluded from the proposed demonstration. That exclusion is an eligibility choice, not a categorical claim that disordered proteins can never participate in crystals. No numerical claim is made about a remaining fraction of the proteome that crystallization would unlock, because the supplied material does not substantiate one.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is reliable transfer from one difficult macromolecule to another. Porous nucleants can help refractory proteins crystallize, but the 2025 review describes dependence on protein properties, pore shape and size, and specific solution conditions. A broadly useful method must accommodate these dependencies through a predictive rule or a bounded set of adjustments. Evidence that one material helps several proteins does not establish that the same intervention will work for an unfamiliar target.

A second barrier is connecting nucleation to diffraction quality. The required outcome is an ordered crystal that supports a validated structure, so a successful protocol must do more than increase the number of nucleation events. It must make useful growth reproducible under specified conditions. The review's emphasis on well-diffracting crystals and condition-dependent nucleation supports treating crystal formation and experimental usability as separate requirements.

Engineering synthesis: the strongest practical version of the innovation would specify which sample properties it requires, which preparation and solution adjustments it permits, and when it predicts failure. Membrane targets add an unresolved compatibility requirement: the environment must support the target while allowing the interactions needed for an ordered lattice. The research names construct engineering, lipid cubic phase methods, and antibody scaffolds as relevant approaches, but the supplied review does not establish their performance or limitations. They therefore remain contextual possibilities, not evidence that broad membrane coverage has been solved. Feasibility of a truly universal nucleant remains uncertain.

current_state.text: The strongest retained evidence is the review by Nanev, Saridakis, and Chayen, published on 7 August 2025. The supplied evidence review reports verified, complete HTML and twelve-page PDF extractions with no recorded extraction issues. It describes protein crystal growth as still largely dependent on trial and error and porous materials as useful aids for some refractory proteins. This is evidence for a continuing bottleneck and meaningful partial progress as documented in 2025.

According to that review's account of the original 2001 mesoporous-silicon study, crystals were obtained from five of six tested proteins; concanavalin A was unsuccessful. This is a concrete example of target-dependent performance. These experimental details are supported here through the retained 2025 review, rather than through an independently inspected copy of the original 2001 paper.

The same review reports that Bioglass induced nucleation under metastable conditions for all seven proteins in a 2006 test, including model proteins and more difficult targets. This was success across the entire reported panel; the supplied evidence does not identify a failed target within that experiment. Seven successes nevertheless establish performance on seven tested proteins, not universality. The review also notes that much experimental work used well-characterized model proteins, with fewer results on difficult targets.

The review further describes 2012 work in which engineered, narrow pore-size distributions showed specificity related to the sizes of the tested proteins. Together with its discussion of protein-dependent pore geometry and required solution conditions, this explains why porous nucleants are a partial tool rather than evidence of an on-demand method for arbitrary macromolecules. It does not prove that a broader transferable protocol is impossible.

The research additionally attributes a universal-substrate aspiration to a 2006 PNAS paper and describes a 2009 review as treating the search for a universal nucleant as continuing. Neither source has retained text in the supplied record. Their attributed wording and detailed claims therefore remain unverified here and are not used as independent evidence for the capability's present status. This access limitation does not establish that the underlying statements are false.

Two listed 2026 sources were used in the research to describe a shift toward high-resolution structural dynamics and continuing case-specific membrane environments. No retained text accompanies either citation, so those descriptions cannot establish the 2026 state in this record. The supplied freshness search record is also empty. The defensible conclusion is that the retained evidence documents substantial limitations in 2025 and does not demonstrate the proposed capability; whether subsequent work changed that situation by 1 November 2026 remains unverified.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: pre-register a panel of at least twenty purified macromolecules with documented failures in standard sparse-matrix screening and applicable seeding trials. Include diverse soluble targets, complexes, and a specified subset of membrane proteins. The stated transferable method should yield diffraction-quality crystals and validated structures across that panel, with independent-laboratory reproduction and deposition of structures and supporting diffraction data. Twenty targets is an author-selected benchmark, not an established scientific threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Independently reproduced structures from at least twenty screening-resistant macromolecules

completion_criteria.text: Proposed controls on predictability: pre-registration should define target selection, sample eligibility, prior failure evidence, membrane environments, permitted construct changes, allowed condition adjustments, and limits on time, sample consumption, and screening effort. It should also state the diffraction and structure-validation requirements before results are known. Seeding requirements should apply where seeds are available or can reasonably be prepared; an initial absence of seeds should not make eligibility logically impossible.
completion_criteria.label: Crystallization follows pre-registered eligibility, effort limits, and validation requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation: success on model proteins alone, appearance of crystals without usable diffraction, or eventual success through an unrestricted search would not meet the intended test. Reporting should include every selected target, failed attempts, protocol deviations, and reproducibility under the declared limits. Intrinsically disordered proteins with no stable domain would remain outside this demonstration. A successful finite panel would establish demonstrated breadth and transferability within those boundaries, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Report all target outcomes and reproducibility under declared limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison with CRX-07, Predictive experimental selection of a chosen crystal form: CRX-11 asks whether a difficult macromolecule can yield a usable crystal; CRX-07 asks whether a chosen form can be selected. These goals are distinguishable even though a nucleant or growth protocol may influence both crystal formation and form selection. CRX-03, Chemical-accuracy prediction of which molecular crystal will form, concerns predicting the outcome rather than experimentally obtaining a diffraction-quality macromolecular crystal. These distinctions follow from the supplied titles; detailed specifications for those entries were not provided.

Roster-based comparison with CRX-13, A growth rulebook that suppresses defects, twins, and disorder in arbitrary crystals: this is the closest overlap in crystal quality. CRX-11 requires sufficient order for diffraction, while CRX-13 explicitly targets defects, twinning, and disorder during growth across a broader class of crystals. A method could contribute to both without making their objectives identical.

Conditional links to CRX-06, Atomic movies of elementary chemical steps without a photo-trigger, and CRX-09, Protonation state as a routine crystallographic observable: crystals supplied by CRX-11 could remove one preparation barrier for eligible macromolecular targets. They would not automatically deliver reaction movies or protonation assignments. Those concepts require their own measurement capabilities and suitable samples. Only their titles were supplied, so more specific dependencies remain unverified.

Roster-based comparison with CRX-01, Atomic-resolution imaging of a single non-crystalline molecule before destruction, and CRX-08, Ab initio atomic structure of matter that exists only once: those entries seek structural information under conditions that do not provide the repeatable crystalline samples pursued here. CRX-02, Chemically complete atomic structures of bulk amorphous solids, and CRX-04, Atomic ensembles measured from total X-ray scattering, likewise concern different sample organizations or structural descriptions. Their common objective is access to difficult structural information; their titles do not establish a requirement for CRX-11's crystallization capability.

Roster-based comparison with CRX-05, Experimental many-electron quantum states of real crystals; CRX-10, Laboratory sources that do facility-class coherent X-ray crystallography; and CRX-12, Continuous atomic-resolution crystallography inside working devices and static extreme environments: these address electronic observables, source capabilities, and measurement environments, respectively. CRX-11 addresses macromolecular sample preparation. Better crystals could be complementary where target classes and experiments overlap, but the supplied roster does not establish a direct dependency or interchangeable solution.

unresolved_issues: No retained evidence establishes whether developments after the August 2025 review changed the capability's status by 1 November 2026.
The PNAS, 2009 review, and two 2026 sources lack retained text; their attributed wording and additional claims remain unverified.
The historical experimental counts are supported through the retained 2025 review, rather than independent inspection of the original experiments.
Universal feasibility, breadth across macromolecular complexes, and compatibility with specified membrane environments remain open.
The proposed demonstration still requires concrete target selection, eligibility rules, membrane preparations, resource budgets, permitted adjustments, and diffraction-validation thresholds.

Detailed relationships with other CRX entries remain provisional because only their titles were supplied. The review's caution about cross-entry guarantees is retained, while the newly supplied roster permits explicitly limited title-based comparisons.

brief.title: Crystals for seeing the shapes of life's molecules
possible: Scientists could reliably grow crystals from purified proteins and other large biological molecules that have resisted earlier attempts. These crystals would let them measure molecular shapes using diffraction, the scattering of X-rays by an ordered structure.
A repeatable preparation method could work across many difficult targets, including groups of molecules bound together and a defined range of proteins that sit in cell membranes.
why: Researchers could study biological structures currently blocked by the difficulty of growing suitable crystals. Each unfamiliar protein would no longer require a separate search for a crystallization recipe.
That would open more targets to studies of how drug molecules bind and how biological structures change during reactions.

sources.showed: This is a study pursuing a universal surface on which protein crystals could begin to form.
sources.cited_for: It represents the ambition to find a broadly useful starting surface for protein crystals.
sources.not_established: An ambition for universal use does not establish predictable crystals suitable for structural measurements.

sources.who: Christo N. Nanev, Emmanuel Saridakis and Naomi E. Chayen
sources.showed: Their review describes how porous materials help difficult proteins form crystals. Tiny pores concentrate protein molecules, and crystals grown this way often scatter X-rays more clearly.
sources.quote: The observation that protein crystals nucleated by means of porous materials often display improved X-ray diffraction is of practical importance for structural studies.
sources.cited_for: Porous materials offer partial success, while protein crystal growth still depends heavily on trial and error.
sources.not_established: The review does not establish a predictable method across difficult proteins, molecular complexes and membrane proteins.

sources.showed: This is a review treating the search for a universal material that starts protein crystal formation as continuing.
sources.cited_for: It describes the continuing search for a broadly transferable way to start crystal formation.
sources.not_established: A review of that search does not demonstrate a broadly reliable crystallization method.

shown: Nanev, Saridakis and Chayen describe a test in which Bioglass, a porous material, started crystal formation for all seven proteins tested, including difficult targets. Their review also describes materials whose effectiveness depended on protein size and pore geometry.
missing: No method has demonstrated reliable transfer across a broad set of difficult biological molecules within fixed limits on adjustments.
Starting crystal formation must reliably lead to ordered crystals that yield validated molecular structures.
Broad coverage of membrane proteins still requires environments that support both the proteins and ordered crystal growth.

milestones.label: Independent laboratories reproduce structures across difficult targets
milestones.explanation: A method would have to yield validated structures from at least twenty previously resistant targets spanning soluble proteins, bound groups and specified membrane proteins, with independent reproduction. This would demonstrate breadth.

milestones.label: Success follows eligibility rules and fixed effort limits
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to define eligible samples, prior failures, membrane conditions, allowed changes, resource limits and structure-quality standards in advance. This would make predictable success distinguishable from unlimited searching.

milestones.label: Every target's outcome and reproducibility are reported
milestones.explanation: Results would have to include every target, failures, departures from the method and repeatability within declared limits, excluding disordered proteins without stable regions. This would establish the method's demonstrated boundaries.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether any crystal-starting material or bounded recipe can work universally.
The required breadth across bound groups of molecules and membrane proteins remains unresolved.
The proposed twenty-target benchmark is a chosen test, rather than an established scientific threshold.

page.title: Universal nucleants for protein crystallization
page.definition: A single nucleant—a material that initiates crystal formation—yields crystals suitable for X-ray structure determination across protein identities, without redesign for each target. Its stated coverage includes soluble proteins, protein complexes and membrane proteins in specified environments.

goal.need: The 2009 Northeast Structural Genomics Consortium results quantify losses between purified protein preparations and deposited X-ray structures. Some preparations diffracted without yielding a structure, so observable diffraction alone was insufficient. The cohort was predominantly bacterial and excluded predicted transmembrane helices and aggregated preparations.

figures.caption: Protein outcomes in the NESG cohort reported in 2009
rows: Diffracted but did not yield structures
figures.note: The last two rows are distinct subsets of the cohort. Selection also excluded proteins with more than 20% low-complexity sequence.

statements.body: The European Commission's FP6 OPTICRYST programme set improved crystallization of difficult proteins as an objective.
statements.quote: Develop and commercialise new, improved methods and equipment to obtain high-quality crystals of proteins difficult to crystallise
statements.context: An objective of grant agreement 37793, which began on 1 December 2006.

statements.body: Imperial College London's nucleant-development team, Govada and colleagues, identifies a universal nucleant as its research direction.
statements.quote: Together with the optimized crystallization conditions, the results are a step forward toward practical synthesis of a readily accessible “universal” nucleant.
statements.context: The reported crystallization experiments tested five proteins against 288 screening conditions.

completion.title: One nucleant yields structure-determining crystals irrespective of protein identity.
completion.criterion: One unchanged nucleant and its specified procedure yield crystals sufficient for X-ray structure determination for every purified, stably folded protein target, including complexes and membrane proteins. Sample eligibility, permitted solution adjustments and membrane environments are fixed before testing; eligibility cannot depend on previous crystallization success. Independent experimental confirmation extends beyond proteins used to develop the nucleant. A finite successful panel establishes only its tested coverage, not literal universality.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; no external universal-nucleant acceptance benchmark was found.
completion.basis: Searches of IUCr and NIH material, prize and benchmark queries, OPTICRYST objectives, and nucleant papers and protocols found no external universality test specifying a panel, success fraction or effort limit. This fallback combines the published universal-nucleant aim with structure determination as the endpoint. The 2014 protocol explicitly leaves success for an unfamiliar protein uncertain.

milestones.title: A nucleant grows protein crystals where untreated controls remain clear for 10 days to 2 weeks.
milestones.criterion: A nucleant produces protein crystals in supersaturated solutions whose untreated controls show no crystals for 10 days to 2 weeks, the protocol's operational test for metastability. Such solutions support growth of existing nuclei. The 2025 review reports porous-silicon success for 5 of 6 proteins in 2001 and Bioglass success for 7 of 7 in 2006. These are experimental panel outcomes, not prescribed success-rate thresholds; they do not establish membrane-protein coverage.
milestones.set_by: Khurshid and colleagues, Nature Protocols (2014), Box 1 and steps 18–21; a protein-crystallization protocol discussing all three tracked classes.
milestones.threshold_quote: if crystals have not appeared within ten days to two weeks, these conditions are considered metastable.

milestones.title: Nucleant-grown protein crystals diffract at least as finely as crystals grown without the nucleant.
milestones.criterion: Nucleant-grown crystals diffract to a resolution at least as fine as the corresponding control crystals; smaller ångström values indicate finer resolved spacings. In a 2011 study of 10 proteins, RECQ1 crystals reached 2.0 Å with molecularly imprinted polymers versus 2.3 Å without them. An HIV protein complex reached 4.2 Å versus a previous 9 Å limit. These comparisons establish soluble-protein and complex results without defining a universal resolution cutoff.
milestones.set_by: Saridakis and colleagues, PNAS (2011), comparative diffraction assessment; the published experiments concerned soluble proteins and protein complexes.
milestones.threshold_quote: resolutions equivalent to or better than their respective controls.

milestones.title: Nucleant-grown protein crystals yield an experimentally determined structure deposited in the PDB.
milestones.criterion: A protein target yields an experimentally determined X-ray structure deposited in the Protein Data Bank, rather than only visible crystals or observable diffraction. This is the success endpoint used by the Northeast Structural Genomics Consortium. A six-protein zeolite study published in 2008 lists deposited structures for PH1033 grown with molecular sieve 5A and TTHB142, with accessions 2hd9 and 2dpn. These examples concern soluble proteins.
milestones.set_by: The structure-determination endpoint used by the Northeast Structural Genomics Consortium in Price and colleagues (2009); applied here to nucleant-grown crystals.
milestones.threshold_quote: success or failure in depositing the construct’s crystal structure into the PDB.

milestones.title: An independent laboratory obtains structures from new targets using the same nucleant across protein classes.
milestones.criterion: A laboratory independent of the developers obtains deposited X-ray structures for previously uncrystallized targets using the same nucleant without target-specific redesign. The demonstration covers each tracked protein class under specified solution and membrane conditions and includes proteins not used to develop the nucleant. This applies the general independent-replication principle to transferability; no external target count or success-rate cutoff was found.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; searches of IUCr and NIH material and the cited development papers and protocol found no independent-transfer benchmark covering these protein classes. NASEM supplies a general replication definition, not this crystallization threshold.

not_found: No external universality benchmark specifying a protein panel, success fraction, screening budget or time limit was found.
No independent transfer study meeting m4 across all three protein classes was identified.
The searches did not identify a deposited membrane-protein structure linked to the cited nucleant experiments.
The full texts of the supplied 2006 PNAS article and 2009 review could not be opened.
The supplied 2026 articles identified by DOI 10.1080/08940886.2026.2649086 and PII S0959440X26000254 could not be opened.
No external completion criterion extending universal protein nucleation to arbitrary macromolecules was found.

results.finding: Human MIF: 1 protein crystallized with imprinted polymers while untreated controls remained clear for at least 2 months.
results.detail: At 1.15 M ammonium sulfate, crystals formed within 8 days with MIF-, lysozyme-, or trypsin-imprinted polymer. The paper identifies these as metastable conditions.
results.quote:
Human MIF. Crystals formed within 8 d at 1.15 M ammonium sul-
fate in the presence of MIF-MIP , L-MIP , and T -MIP (Fig. 1). All
other trials remained clear for at least 2 mo.

results.finding: For 1 membrane protein, AcrB, nanogels produced crystals while controls remained clear for at least 2 weeks.
results.detail: Working phase diagrams identified crystal formation under metastable conditions. The study used hydroxyl-functionalised nanogels and AcrB in a detergent-containing solution.
results.quote: The diagrams showed that the addition of NGOHs resulted in crystal formation at metastable conditions just below the supersolubility curve, where the control drops remained clear for at least two weeks.

results.finding: In a study of 8 proteins, SDB1-grown concanavalin A crystals diffracted to 1.54 Å.
results.detail: The concanavalin A control diffracted to 2.10 Å. Results varied: proteinase K crystals diffracted to 1.20 Å with SDB1 versus 1.19 Å in the control.
results.quote: Concanavalin A (1.54 Å with SDB1 vs 2.10 Å without SDB1)

results.finding: One HIV protein complex produced L-MIP-grown crystals that diffracted to 4.2 Å.
results.detail: Previous crystallization attempts reached no finer than 9 Å. Each tested protein-condition combination was repeated in at least six drops.
results.quote:
Trials in the presence of L-MIP produced
crystals that diffracted up to 4.2 Å.

results.finding: One topo IV–DNA–delafloxacin complex produced a graphene-PEG-nucleated structure at 2.0 Å.
results.detail: The text reports a 2.4 Å structure for the V-site complex but does not explicitly identify it as grown without nucleant, so the required control comparison is not established.
results.quote:
Moreover, a V18 structure solved at an unprecedented 2.0 Å resolution
(Fig. 4, Supplementary Table 1) was obtained by improving the crystal
quality through seeding with a graphene-PEG nucleant 35.

results.finding: Tb–Xo4-grown crystals yielded a PDB-deposited structure for 1 soluble protein, pb9 (5MF2), among 8 proteins tested.
results.detail: The pb9 crystals were grown with Tb–Xo4 under nucleating conditions and then soaked in a more concentrated solution for experimental phasing.
results.quote:
A superimposition of our monomer (PDB entry ; 5MF2) on the PDB entry ; 4JMQ monomer
34
led to a root mean square deviation of 0.55 Å, showing that the binding of Tb–Xo4 does not modify the overall structure of the protein.

results.finding: One topo IV–DNA cleavage complex yielded a graphene-nucleant-grown X-ray structure at 2.0 Å.
results.detail: The V-site complex was crystallized with a graphene-PEG nucleant; its structure is identified as PDB 8QMB.
results.quote:
Moreover, a V18 structure solved at an unprecedented 2.0 Å resolution
(Fig. 4, Supplementary Table 1) was obtained by improving the crystal
quality through seeding with a graphene-PEG nucleant 35.

results.finding: Bacteriorhodopsin: 1 membrane protein yielded a deposited X-ray structure, PDB 1BRR.
results.detail: The crystals were heterogeneously nucleated on benzamidine sulfate crystals. The X-ray structure was determined at 2.9 Å resolution.
results.quote:
Data deposition: The coordinates and structure factors reported in this
paper have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank, Biology Department,
Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY 11973 (PDB ID code 1BRR).
